analysis.one_liner: Caps US prices of drugs developed with federal research money at prices charged abroad.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would cap prices of taxpayer-funded drugs at the median price in Canada and six other wealthy countries, never left committee and died without a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Any drug, vaccine, or medical device developed with federal research funding would have to be sold in the US at a price no higher than the median price in Canada and six other large, high-income countries. Companies taking federal research money would have to sign a pricing agreement with the Department of Health and Human Services, report their clinical trial costs and revenues, and get a public process to obtain any waiver. The bill never received a hearing or a vote in the House Energy and Commerce Committee and died when the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients and taxpayers who pay for prescription drugs, especially those on newer drugs and therapies developed with NIH or other federal funding. Americans currently often pay far more than patients in Canada, France, Germany, and other wealthy countries for the same drug.
analysis.who_benefits_short: US patients and taxpayers buying prescription drugs

how_it_helps.text: The bill requires every federal research grant, contract, or patent license for a biomedical product to include a reasonable-price agreement, so the public pays no more than the median price in Canada and six other reference countries for products it helped fund.

The bill also makes HHS publish companies' clinical trial costs, federal subsidies, and annual revenue reports for federally funded products, so the public can see what these drugs actually cost to develop.
Any waiver from the price cap would require public notice, a comment period, a public hearing, and a published economic analysis, rather than a private deal.

analysis.who_pays: Pharmaceutical and biotech companies that develop or license products built on federally funded research would give up the ability to charge Americans the highest prices in the world on those products. Patients might also see slightly less industry willingness to take on some federally funded projects.
analysis.who_pays_short: Drug and biotech firms using federal research

drawbacks.text: The industry's strongest objection is that capping US prices at foreign medians could reduce the return on new drugs and discourage investment in biomedical R&D; the bill itself acknowledges the need to keep 'robust incentives to invest in biomedical research and development' and lets HHS consider that in its rules.

The bill's price cap applies only to products developed with federal research funding or federally licensed patents and data, so most drugs priced high today would not be directly covered, and HHS could waive the requirement 'in the public interest.'
Defining a reasonable price by formula is administratively hard where third parties control the intellectual property, a challenge the bill directs regulators to work through.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is direct and concrete: Americans would stop paying the developed world's highest prices for drugs their own tax dollars paid to develop. The costs are real but narrower than industry claims, since the bill covers only federally funded products and preserves R&D incentives by instruction. The main weakness is scope, not design: most expensive drugs fall outside it.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee in May 2023 and sent to its Health subcommittee, which never took it up, so it never came to a floor vote before the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Representative Val Hoyle introduced the bill on May 5, 2023 with 14 original cosponsors.
It was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the day it was introduced, and on May 12, 2023 referred to the Subcommittee on Health.
No further action was recorded; the bill never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Drug and biotech companies that developed or licensed federally funded products kept charging US patients more than patients in other wealthy countries, with no competitive pressure from the bill. Members of Congress faced no recorded vote on the issue.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Drugmakers keeping US prices the world's highest

for.name: Rep. Val Hoyle
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill requiring reasonable pricing agreements on taxpayer-funded biomedical products.

for.name: 18 House cosponsors
for.role: Original and additional cosponsors, all Democrats (Doggett, DeLauro, Jayapal, Khanna, Pocan, Schakowsky, and others)
for.what_they_did: Signed on in support, giving the bill 19 total House sponsors and cosponsors.

sides.party_line_note: All 19 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican signed on, and the committee that held the bill was chaired by Republicans, so the bill never advanced past referral.

industries.note: The bill would cap prices of federally funded drugs at the median foreign price and force disclosure of trial costs and revenues, directly cutting the excess US pricing that makes America the most profitable drug market in the world. Its interest ran against the patients and taxpayers it prices against.
